title: Hyde Park Now
voiceover: On June 19, 2026, the Obama Presidential Center opened to the public. Juneteenth, the day that marks the end of slavery in America. The night before, an invitation-only dedication brought Bruce Springsteen and Stevie Wonder to the lawn, with former presidents in the crowd. Then the doors opened on Jackson Park. This is the same ground Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux laid out in 1871. It's the same ground that held the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, the White City that drew twenty-seven million visitors to the lakefront. A century and a third later, a new institution sits on it. The date was chosen on purpose. Juneteenth, on the South Side where Barack Obama once worked as a community organizer, for a center built to honor the first Black president. The campus runs 19.3 acres. The firm Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects designed it, with the park landscape shaped by Michael Van Valkenburgh. At the center stands a stone museum tower that rises about 225 feet, its sides carved with words drawn from Black history. On the north face, the artist Julie Mehretu set 35 glass panels she calls Uprising of the Sun, inspired by the marches from Selma to Montgomery. The whole thing cost roughly 850 million dollars in private money. No presidential center has ever cost that much. Inside there's a museum, a branch of the Chicago Public Library, a forum building for public events, an athletic center, and the offices of the Obama Foundation. Getting here took ten years, and it was not smooth. The Obamas chose Chicago over New York and Honolulu in 2016. Then came the wait. Because Jackson Park is an Olmsted landscape listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the project couldn't just break ground. It needed a full federal review, the kind that weighs whether a public works project will damage a historic place. That review ran for years. And while it ran, a group called Protect Our Parks went to court to stop the whole thing. They were a small group of residents, but they pushed hard. They argued that handing 19 acres of public parkland to a private foundation broke the public trust that's supposed to keep parks open to everyone. They argued the study of alternative sites was a sham, written to reach a conclusion the city had already chosen. They argued the city had effectively given away land that belonged to all of Chicago. They lost, again and again. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up an early appeal. A federal judge dismissed the core suit in 2022. The federal review itself admitted, in plain language, that the Center would alter the historic character of an Olmsted park. The courts let it proceed anyway. The Obamas, Governor J.B. Pritzker, and Mayor Lori Lightfoot broke ground together on September 28, 2021. From there it was just under five years of construction to the ribbon. The argument the Protect Our Parks suits raised never really got answered. It just got overruled. Now hold that opening day in your mind, and look west, at the streets just past the park. That's Woodlawn. It's the neighborhood that organized for years to bring this here, that wanted the jobs and the foot traffic and the pride of it. And while the tower went up, Woodlawn got more expensive. Not a little. On the east side of Woodlawn, the blocks closest to the Center, the median price of a single-family home doubled between 2019 and 2025, to about 440,000 dollars. That's the figure from DePaul's Institute for Housing Studies. Pull the lens back to the city's whole Jackson Park housing pilot area, and the change is starker. The median sale price went from 72,500 dollars in 2016, the year the site was announced, to 330,000 dollars by 2025. More than four times higher in nine years. And the supply of homes a working family could actually afford fell off a cliff. In 2024, less than a third of the housing stock nearby still counted as affordable. Fifteen years before, it had been roughly two-thirds. The city saw this coming. Organizers saw it years out. In September 2020, after a campaign of about five years, the City Council passed the Woodlawn Housing Preservation Ordinance. On paper it was real protection. It reserved 52 city-owned vacant lots for affordable housing. It set up a loan fund, home-repair grants for longtime owners, and a right of first refusal that was supposed to give tenants a shot at buying their building before it sold out from under them. Then six years passed. And in May 2026, the Illinois Answers Project went and checked what the ordinance had actually delivered. The results were thin. Of the 52 reserved lots, exactly one project had been finished, a single building of 58 units. The tenant right of first refusal, the one tool meant to let renters buy before a sale, had generated zero notices in five years. A home-improvement grant program reached just 36 longtime homeowners, about 20,000 dollars each. And roughly 2 million dollars set aside to preserve and rehab housing sat completely unspent, in part because almost no one applied and no one inside the city was clearly assigned to push the money out the door. The protections were real on paper. On the ground, they barely slowed the wave. The people the ordinance was written to keep in place were leaving while the money it promised them sat in an account. To understand why a doubling of home prices lands so hard in a place like Woodlawn, you have to know how Black families in Chicago came to own homes in the first place. For decades, redlining and racial covenants shut them out of ordinary bank mortgages. The loans that built white wealth in the suburbs were simply not on offer. So when Black families finally bought, on the South and West Sides, a huge share of them bought on contract. A contract sale looked like a mortgage and worked nothing like one. A speculator would buy a house cheap from a fleeing white owner, then turn around and sell it to a Black family at a steep markup, on terms the family had no power to refuse. The seller kept the deed until the very last payment was made, years down the line. The buyer built no equity along the way, and got none of the protections a real mortgage carried. And miss a single payment, even one, and the seller could evict and keep everything already paid, then sell the same house to the next family and start the whole cycle again. Families took in boarders and worked second jobs just to make the monthly number. In North Lawndale, more than three-quarters of the homes sold to Black buyers between 1950 and 1970 were sold this way, at an average markup of 84 percent over what a white buyer paid for a comparable house. People fought back. In 1968, North Lawndale residents formed the Contract Buyers League. A World War II veteran named Clyde Ross helped lead it. Around 500 families went on a payment strike, holding their money in escrow until the sellers renegotiated, and roughly 450 of them eventually won new terms. But the fight was house by house, and the larger machine kept running. Researchers at Duke University's Samuel DuBois Cook Center on Social Equity later put a number on the total damage. Contract selling stripped between 3 and 4 billion dollars from Black Chicago. That was money that should have become equity, a paid-off house, a down payment for a grandchild, something handed down. Instead it flowed to the sellers, and for the families it simply vanished. You can still measure the hole it left, decades on. In 2022, the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances found that the median white family in America held about 285,000 dollars in wealth. The median Black family held about 45,000. That's a gap of more than six to one. And here's the part that surprises people. Black wealth actually rose over those years. The gap grew anyway, because white wealth rose faster, off a much bigger base. That's what makes a wealth gap so stubborn. You can run hard and still fall further behind. A gap that wide doesn't come from one bad decade or one set of choices. It gets built one stripped contract, one denied loan, one priced-out block at a time, and then it gets passed down, the way wealth is, in reverse. The family that lost a contract house in 1962 didn't just lose a house. It lost the thing that house would have become, the inheritance, the cushion, the down payment for the next generation. And the pattern under all of it is older than anyone now living it. Paul Cornell bought these blocks in 1853 and sold the idea of a refined lakefront suburb, with wide lots and a fast train downtown. The 1893 fair brought the crowds and the prestige. The University of Chicago rose nearby in the 1890s, funded by John D. Rockefeller, and it never stopped growing. In the 1950s and 60s it backed the urban renewal that bulldozed swaths of Hyde Park and Kenwood and pushed thousands of families out, much of it Black families, all of it carried out in the name of saving the neighborhood. Then in our own decade the university kept moving south across the Midway into Woodlawn, with new dorms and acquired property, the same direction the prices were rising. Now the Obama Center sits at the edge of it all. Each time, across a hundred and seventy years, the shape is the same. A powerful institution arrives, the ground around it gains value, and the people already there are left to wonder whether the place they helped build still has room for them. A hundred and seventy-three years after Cornell first walked these blocks, the question underneath this whole neighborhood, who this ground is really for, still isn't settled.
